title: Righteous in his generation (Genesis 6:9)
hookLine: the rabbis argue whether Noah was great in any age or only beside his neighbors

cards: Ten generations from Adam to Noah, the Mishnah counts, and things have gone badly: the earth, the Torah says, is filled with violence. Then one sentence about one man.
Noah was, in his generations, a man righteous and wholehearted. "Noah walked with God." Pure praise?
Picture the best student in a class where everyone else stopped showing up. Great, or just great by comparison? The rabbis caught one Hebrew word, bedorotav, in his generations, and started to argue.

teach.b: Tzaddik: a righteous person. It comes from tzedek, justice, rightness, things set straight, the same root as tzedakah, the giving you met on day sixteen. Now the argument.
The Talmud records two teachers, Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish, reading the phrase in opposite ways.
One says it's criticism: he was righteous only compared to them; in Abraham's day, nobody would have noticed him.
The other says it's praise: if he stayed good in a generation like that, with no one to learn from, imagine him among good people.
Rashi, the great medieval commentator, sets both readings side by side and doesn't pick. The tradition keeps both, because both are true of people. Some are good because everyone around them is.
Some are good in spite of everyone around them. And from the inside, it's hard to know which one you are. Another small detail.
Noah walked with God; later, Abraham speaks of the God before whom he walks. Rashi says Noah needed God beside him to hold him up, while Abraham could walk ahead on his own.
Not an insult: an honest picture of a man doing his best.
And the Talmud says every generation has at least thirty-six righteous people.
Later folk tradition made them hidden, unknown even to themselves: tzaddikim nobody would ever put in a book.

how: Jews read the story of Noah each autumn as the weekly Torah portion Noach, and the rabbinic argument over "in his generations" is a favorite text for study and sermons that week.

o: a teacher who leads a school of students
a person who does what is right and just
a saint who never does anything wrong

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: giving to the poor, as justice

s: the rabbis all agree Noah was a perfect hero
the Talmud records two readings: praise for staying good in a bad age, and criticism that he was good only by comparison.
tzedakah, the word for giving to the poor, comes from the same root as tzaddik
both come from tzedek, justice. giving is the right thing, not an optional extra.
Rashi picks one reading and rejects the other
he sets both side by side and keeps them.

games.q: you're a rabbi reading "Noah was in his generations a man righteous." what do those three words, in his generations, mean?
o: praise: he stayed good in a terrible age.
criticism: he was good only by comparison.
games.why: the Talmud records both readings, and Rashi repeats both without choosing. the argument is part of the teaching.

practice: Think of the people around you this week, at work, at home, online, and how much they shape what you do.
Then hold in mind one right thing you could do that nobody will see: returning something, fixing what someone else broke, a kind word about someone who isn't there.
If you pray, you can ask for the strength to be good where you are.

wordCard.voice: Tzaddik. A righteous person, from tzedek, justice. Genesis gives the word to Noah.

orig.note: Hebrew: a righteous person, from tzedek, justice.

carryVoice: Your line: good where you are. Not better than the room, just right in the room you're in. That's day thirty-two.
